_comment: USER-FACING highlights for the release named by `version`, published to the website as
part of https://devicechain.io/releases.json (see hack/build-release-manifest.sh).
🔴 UPDATE THIS IN THE PR THAT PREPARES A RELEASE, BEFORE TAGGING — and update `version`,
`theme`, `breaking` and `highlights` TOGETHER. They are one record of one release, and
the way this file goes wrong is three of the four moving while the fourth keeps last
release's answer: a theme naming work that is not in the highlights below it reads as
confidently as one that is. The `guard` job fails
the release when `version` does not match the tag, deliberately and as the FIRST job —
so a forgotten update costs nothing but a re-run, rather than publishing last release's
highlights against this release's version. Confidently wrong is worse than absent, and
this file is the one part of the manifest a machine cannot derive.
`theme` IS THE ONE PHRASE THAT NAMES THE RELEASE — a chapter title, not a changelog
line. It leads the GitHub release notes and it reaches releases.json, so it is the
first thing a reader decides against. A good one names what changed about the system:
"the instance is declared, not remembered". A bad one is a category ("bug fixes and
improvements"), the version restated, or the first highlight with its verbs filed off —
if it would fit any release, it is not this release's theme.
Write a PHRASE. The guard caps it at 72 characters, the width of a commit subject,
because past that you are writing a sentence, and a sentence about what changed is a
highlight — there is already a list for those below. The cap is the only taste this
file can enforce; the rest is on you.
🔴 The theme is PUBLISHED, and so is every highlight — into the GitHub release body and
into devicechain.io/releases.json. No ADR references in either: ADRs live in a repo the
reader cannot open, so a citation is a dead reference dressed as a source. Say the thing
itself, or link to a public page. THIS BLOCK IS DIFFERENT — `_comment` is published
nowhere, it is the only part of the file a reader never sees, and it may cite ADR-080 or
any other freely. The guard reads exactly that distinction: it scans `theme` and
`highlights[]`, case-insensitively, and leaves this block alone.
WRITE FOR SOMEONE DECIDING WHETHER TO UPGRADE, not for someone reading the commit log.
The changelog is already generated from commit subjects and is right there in the release
notes; repeating `fix(events): give payload rows and anchors identities of their own` here
adds nothing. Say what changed for the person running the platform.
Keep it to a handful of lines. This renders in the website's download menu, not in a
document — a fifteen-item list is a changelog wearing a different hat.
`breaking` MEANS 'THIS RELEASE HAS BREAKING CHANGES'. It does NOT mean 'you must recreate
your instance', and this comment used to say it did — it told you to set the flag when an
upgrade is not a plain `helm upgrade`. The website has not read it that way since the
copy was repaired: `true` renders exactly one sentence, 'This release has breaking changes
— read the release notes before upgrading', and `false` renders nothing at all. So set it
true whenever something breaks for SOMEBODY — an API caller, an operator, a package
consumer — and use the first highlight to say who, and whether the upgrade itself is
ordinary. If a release ever genuinely requires recreating an instance, give that its OWN
manifest field rather than overloading this one a second time.
The other correction: there is no docs banner. Nothing under docs/ fetches releases.json.
The website download menu is this file's only consumer.
For each highlight, ask whether it makes a sentence on the marketing site stale. The
site is a separate repository and nothing here reads its prose. Answering "no site
impact" is a fine answer; not asking is not.
theme: each area signs in to the broker as itself, and releases are signed
highlights: Four groups are affected. A site running the edge agent must move to the agent's gateway identity: the old direct-device uplink is removed, and a leftover `agentId` stops the agent at start. A script or integration that read a device's access token back from the credential queries now receives a fingerprint, because the token is stored as a keyed digest and shown once; set a new token to get one you can load onto the device. A device program on the C# SDK whose connection the broker refuses now gets `MqttConnectRefusedException`, and a session's reconnect loop stops, where it used to retry the refused credential indefinitely. An installation that runs the chart without `dcctl` needs the instance namespace and the broker administrator's Secret in place before its first install, or `brokerAdmin.enabled=false`. The upgrade from v0.24.0 is in place (`dcctl install`, then `dcctl upgrade`) but is run twice: the first gives every area a broker login of its own and keeps the shared `dc_service` login, and the second retires it, and does so only when the first ended Ready. Each rolls the broker once, one server at a time under `--ha`. Roll forward, not back: `v0.24.0` refuses the instance configuration the first upgrade writes and cannot look up a digested access token, so a failed upgrade is fixed by running `dcctl upgrade` again. From v0.22.0 or earlier, upgrade through v0.23.0 and v0.24.0 first. Three migrations add five tables, a column and their indexes and rewrite no row; separately, `device-management` converts every stored access token to its digest on start, and while the services roll, devices that authenticate with a token can fail to connect until every `device-management` pod runs v0.25.0.

This is the first signed release. Every service image, the operator, the edge agent, the broker administrator and the console, and the Helm chart, are signed with cosign (keyless, bound to the release workflow and the tag), and each image carries a signed SBOM and SLSA build provenance. `hack/verify-release-signatures.sh <tag>` checks all of it with no key to obtain, and ends with two checks that must fail for it to pass. Releases before v0.25.0 carry no signature. The database image is not covered yet.

Every area signs in to the message broker as itself. Until now all services shared one login, so any pod could present the credential of all of them. Each area now has a login in a Secret only that area mounts, held to the streams, consumers, buckets and reply subjects it declares. One administration login, run as a job before every install and upgrade, alone creates and changes streams and buckets; a service only checks them and refuses to start, naming what differs, and `dcctl broker reconcile` repairs one. The cache buckets' lifetime is now fixed at five minutes, a replica count raised in the instance configuration takes effect at the next upgrade, and the new `dc-broker-admin` image must be reachable from a mirrored registry.

A device's access token is now stored as a keyed digest, never as sent, so a database or backup leak yields no working token. The token is shown once, when it is set, and existing tokens keep working. Changing a credential's type to or from `ACCESS_TOKEN` must name `credentialId` in the same request, and a token over 256 bytes is refused.

The edge agent is now a gateway: an ordinary device of its own that the platform lets speak only for the devices assigned to it, in a namespace of its own. An event for a device that is not assigned is refused loudly: it is recorded with its payload, counted in `resolve_not_gateway_child_total`, and the agent is sent a notice and keeps the event in a local file. Upgrade the platform, including the broker, before you restart any agent on this version.

Integrations no longer need a person's sign-in. A tenant administrator creates a service account under Settings, and the integration obtains five-minute access tokens with the OAuth `client_credentials` grant, holding exactly the roles and customer scope it was given. Over-the-air updates can also be rolled out to a device group: never more than `maxInFlight` devices with an unfinished update, with pause, resume, abort and an optional failure threshold that pauses the rollout by itself.

Smaller changes: `dcctl bootstrap` and `dcctl upgrade` take `--values`, a tuning file the instance records and every later upgrade applies again; an entity's audit entry is now saved in the same transaction as the change, so a failed entry means the change is not made; tenant deletion exposes which storage system is holding it back, with three new alerts; dashboards gain an absolute time range, a history table with CSV and PNG download, explained empty states, and a kiosk playlist at `/dash?rotate=...&every=...`; and the 1.0 versioning policy and security model are published.
